summary: Defines the profile for Route Origin Authorizations. A ROA is a signed object proving that the holder of an address block has authorized a particular AS to originate routes for prefixes in that block. It is a standards-track document that was replaced by RFC 9582.

eli5.summary: A ROA is a signed permission slip saying "this network may announce this address block". This defines what goes in the slip. It was later replaced by RFC 9582.

questions: what is maxlength in a roa
subtitle: The signed object that lets an address holder say which AS may announce its prefixes.

tldr.problem: Routing security needs a way to verify that an Autonomous System has been given permission by the holder of an address block to advertise routes to prefixes within it.
tldr.mechanism: A Route Origin Authorization (ROA) is an RPKI signed object that names one AS number and a list of IP prefixes, each with an optional maxLength, wrapped in the CMS-based signed object template.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6482 was obsoleted by RFC 9582, which is the current ROA profile.

today: RFC 6482 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 9582, which is the current definition of the ROA profile.

sections.title: What a ROA Is For
sections.content:
The primary purpose of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is to improve routing security. As part of it, entities need a way to verify that an AS has permission from an IP address block holder to advertise routes to prefixes within that block. A ROA provides this.

A ROA uses the generic RPKI signed object template, which supplies a CMS wrapper and a general validation procedure. This RFC completes the specification by defining three things: the OID that marks the object as a ROA, the ASN.1 syntax of its content (encoded with DER), and one extra validation step.
sections.eli5: It is a permission slip from the owner of an address block saying which network may announce it. The RFC defines what the slip looks like.

sections.title: The ROA Content
sections.content:
The content type is called routeOriginAuthz, with the numerical value 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.24. This OID MUST appear both in the eContentType and in the content-type signed attribute.

The content, RouteOriginAttestation, identifies a single AS and a list of one or more IP prefixes. It has three fields: version (which MUST be 0), asID (the AS number authorized to originate routes) and ipAddrBlocks. If the holder wants to authorize several ASes for the same prefixes, it issues several ROAs, one per AS number.

Each address family entry carries an addressFamily, which MUST be 0001 (IPv4) or 0002 (IPv6), and a list of prefixes. ROAs represent only prefixes, which is more restrictive than the arbitrary ranges that RFC 3779 can express.
sections.eli5: The slip says one thing: this network number may announce these address blocks. If two networks are allowed, you write two slips.

sections.title: Prefixes and maxLength
sections.content:
Each prefix may have an optional maxLength. If present, it MUST be at least the prefix length and at most the address length in bits (32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6). It is the longest, most specific prefix the AS may advertise. Without it, the AS may advertise only the exact prefix.

The RFC's example: for the prefix 203.0.113/24 with a maxLength of 26, the AS may advertise 203.0.113/24, 203.0.113.128/25 or 203.0.113.0/25, but not 203.0.113.0/27.

A ROA may contain a prefix covered by another prefix in the same ROA. It MAY contain two elements with the identical prefix, but this is NOT RECOMMENDED, because the one with the shorter maxLength grants nothing extra.
sections.eli5: maxLength says how finely the network may slice the address block. A limit of 26 means it may cut it into pieces, but not into tiny slivers smaller than that.

sections.title: Validating a ROA
sections.content: Before a relying party uses a ROA to judge a routing announcement, it MUST validate the ROA. It performs all the checks of the signed object template and one more: the IP address delegation extension from RFC 3779 must be present in the end-entity (EE) certificate inside the ROA, and every prefix in the ROA must lie within the addresses in that extension.
sections.eli5: Before trusting a slip, check that the signer really owns the addresses written on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A ROA is not confidential. It is expected to be stored in repositories open to all ISPs and perhaps all Internet users. It carries no explicit authentication and no non-repudiation: the PKI provides authorization, not authentication.

Its integrity MUST be established. The signer's right to authorize the AS comes from the address and AS number PKI: one MUST verify the signature using an X.509 certificate issued under this PKI and check that the prefixes match the certificate's address space extension. ROAs also inherit the security considerations of the signed object template and of CMS.
sections.eli5: Anyone may read the slip. What matters is that nobody can change it, and that it was signed by the real owner.
